entries.t: Humanity's oldest companion, domesticated from wolves more than 15,000 years ago. Its nose holds up to 300 million scent receptors.
entries.f: There are hundreds of breeds — every new breed you scan is logged as a new form.

entries.t: A silent stalker that has lived alongside people for about 10,000 years, first earning its keep by hunting grain-stealing rodents.
entries.f: Cats can swivel each ear independently using 32 muscles.

entries.t: A twitchy-nosed grazer whose eyes sit high on the sides of its head, giving it a nearly all-round view to spot predators.
entries.f: A rabbit's teeth never stop growing — chewing hay keeps them worn down.

entries.t: Stuffs food into stretchy cheek pouches that reach back to its shoulders, then hauls the stash home to its burrow.
entries.f: Most pet hamsters are nocturnal and can run several kilometres a night on a wheel.

entries.t: A chatty rodent from the Andes that squeaks, purrs and "wheeks" to its herd. Happy ones leap straight up in a hop called "popcorning".
entries.f: Like humans, guinea pigs can't make their own vitamin C and must get it from food.

entries.t: Bred from wild carp in China over 1,000 years ago, it now shimmers in ponds and bowls across the globe.
entries.f: Goldfish memories last months, not three seconds — they can be trained to respond to sounds and colours.

entries.t: A long, bendy hunter built to chase prey down burrows. Its wild cousin, the black-footed ferret, was once thought to be extinct.
entries.f: Excited ferrets do a bouncing, sideways hop known as the "weasel war dance".

entries.t: A brilliant mimic that can learn hundreds of words and use some of them with apparent meaning.
entries.f: Alex, a famous African grey, learned to name colours and shapes and count up to six.

entries.t: An ancient survivor whose roach-like ancestors scuttled about over 300 million years ago. It can flatten itself to squeeze through gaps thinner than a coin.
entries.f: Of about 4,600 cockroach species, only around 30 live alongside people as pests.

entries.t: A buzzing acrobat that tastes with its feet and sees the world through thousands of lenses in each compound eye.
entries.f: Flies process images so fast that a swatter seems to move in slow motion to them.

entries.t: A gentle grazer with a four-chambered stomach that re-chews its food as cud to squeeze out every nutrient.
entries.f: Cows form close friendships and show signs of stress when separated from their favourite herd-mates.

entries.t: A powerful runner that can doze standing up by locking its legs. Its eyes are among the largest of any land mammal.
entries.f: Horses can't breathe through their mouths — only through their noses.

entries.t: A clever snuffler that roots through soil with its sensitive snout. Pigs wallow in mud to keep cool because they barely sweat.
entries.f: Pigs have learned to play simple video games using a joystick.

entries.t: A flocking grazer whose wool keeps growing all its life. The curling horns of a ram grow bigger every year.
entries.f: Sheep can recognise at least 50 other sheep faces and remember them for years.

entries.t: Descended from the red junglefowl, it is now the most numerous bird on Earth — there are more chickens than people.
entries.f: Proteins from a T. rex fossil most closely matched those of chickens and ostriches.

entries.t: The dabbling duck behind almost every farm duck breed. Males flash an iridescent green head; females wear camouflaging brown.
entries.f: Its feathers are waterproofed with oil from a gland near the base of the tail.

entries.t: A loud, loyal bird that often mates for life and fiercely guards its goslings with hisses and wing-slaps.
entries.f: Migrating geese fly in a V so each bird rides the updraft from the wingtip ahead.

entries.h: Rice paddies and wetlands of Asia
entries.t: A mighty wallower that pulls ploughs through flooded paddies. Its rich milk makes true mozzarella.
entries.f: There are around 200 million domestic water buffalo in the world.

entries.t: A sure-footed pack animal of the Andes. When annoyed it may spit — mostly at other llamas.
entries.f: Farmers use llamas to guard sheep because they boldly confront foxes and coyotes.

entries.t: A long-legged sprinter that relies on speed rather than burrows, bursting away at up to 70 km/h.
entries.f: Unlike rabbits, baby hares are born furred with eyes open, ready to run.

entries.t: A plump little ground bird that prefers to run and hide in the grass, exploding into flight only when startled.
entries.f: Each female Japanese quail lays eggs with her own consistent speckle pattern.

entries.t: A round, rust-faced game bird that lives in family groups called coveys, huddling together on cold nights.
entries.f: Grey partridge chicks eat mostly insects during their first weeks of life.

entries.t: A bushy-tailed acrobat that buries thousands of nuts each autumn and finds many of them again by memory and smell.
entries.f: Forgotten nuts sprout into trees — squirrels are accidental forest planters.

entries.h: Lawns and woodland of North America
entries.t: A red-breasted thrush that tilts its head on lawns, watching and listening for earthworms before it pounces.
entries.f: A robin can eat around 4 metres of earthworms in a single day.

entries.h: Towns and deserts of North America
entries.t: A cheerful songbird whose males glow red on the head and chest. The redder the male, the more females like him.
entries.f: The red comes from pigments in its food — a better diet means a brighter bird.

entries.h: Gardens and meadows of Europe & Asia
entries.t: A jewel-bright finch with a red face and golden wing bars that plucks seeds from thistles with its fine beak.
entries.f: A flock of goldfinches is called a "charm".

entries.h: Forests and gardens of North America
entries.t: A slate-grey sparrow that flashes white outer tail feathers as it hops. Its winter arrival earned it the nickname "snowbird".
entries.f: Juncos are among the most abundant forest birds in North America.

entries.t: A tiny, fearless bird that calls its own name: "chick-a-dee-dee-dee". More "dees" means a bigger threat nearby.
entries.f: Each autumn chickadees grow new brain cells to help remember where they hid their food.

entries.t: A bold, noisy member of the crow family that can mimic the scream of a hawk to scare rivals away from food.
entries.f: A single jay may bury thousands of acorns in autumn, helping oak forests spread.

entries.t: A sleek black-and-white corvid with a long, glossy tail and a famously sharp mind.
entries.f: In 2008 Eurasian magpies became the first non-mammals shown to recognise themselves in a mirror.

entries.h: Gardens and scrub of Asia & Africa
entries.t: A crested songbird with a bubbly, liquid call, common in gardens across Asia and Africa.
entries.f: The red-vented bulbul is so adaptable it now lives on islands from Hawaii to Fiji.

entries.t: An orange-breasted finch that breeds in the far north and pours south in winter to feast on beech nuts.
entries.f: Some winter roosts of bramblings hold millions of birds.

entries.t: The male looks brilliant blue, yet has no blue pigment at all — the structure of its feathers scatters light.
entries.f: Indigo buntings migrate at night and can navigate by the stars.

entries.t: A hovering jewel whose wings can beat up to 80 times a second. It can even fly backwards.
entries.f: The bee hummingbird of Cuba is the world's smallest bird, about 5 cm long.

entries.t: A slow wanderer carrying its spiral home on its back, gliding on a ribbon of slime that protects its soft foot.
entries.f: Snails scrape food with a tongue-like ribbon covered in thousands of microscopic teeth.

entries.t: A snail that gave up its shell. It breathes through a hole in its side called a pneumostome.
entries.f: Slugs have four tentacles — the upper pair carries eyes, the lower pair smells and tastes.

entries.h: Woodland, farms and suburbs of the Americas
entries.t: A striped stinker that warns before it sprays — stamping its feet and raising its tail. Its spray can hit a target 3 metres away.
entries.f: People can smell skunk spray from more than a kilometre away.

entries.t: A slow, prickly rodent armoured with up to 30,000 quills that detach on contact and lodge in a predator's skin.
entries.f: Hedgehogs look similar but aren't rodents at all — they're closer kin to shrews and moles.

entries.t: A spotted beetle whose bright shell warns birds that it tastes awful. Gardeners love it as natural pest control.
entries.f: A single ladybug can eat around 5,000 aphids in its lifetime.

entries.t: A busy pollinator. Honey bees tell their hive-mates where to find flowers by performing a "waggle dance".
entries.f: About one in every three bites of food we eat depends on pollinators like bees.

entries.t: A tiny superorganism living in colonies of up to millions. Ants communicate by laying invisible trails of scent.
entries.f: Some ants can carry 10 to 50 times their own body weight.

entries.t: A powerful jumper that can leap 20 times its body length, then snap open its wings to glide away.
entries.f: Grasshoppers hear with "ears" on their bellies, just behind their legs.

entries.t: A night singer that chirps by rubbing a ridged file on one wing against a scraper on the other.
entries.f: Count a snowy tree cricket's chirps in 13 seconds and add 40 to get the temperature in °F.

entries.t: An ambush hunter that waits motionless, then snatches prey with spiked forelegs faster than you can blink.
entries.f: A mantis can swivel its head 180 degrees to look over its shoulder.

entries.t: The loudest insect on Earth — males buzz by buckling drum-like plates called tymbals on their abdomens.
entries.f: Periodical cicadas spend 13 or 17 years underground, then all emerge at once.

entries.t: A tiny sap-sipper that springs away like a flea when disturbed, many dressed in dazzling stripes.
entries.f: Leafhoppers "talk" to each other by sending vibrations through plant stems.

entries.t: A delicate insect with glassy, net-veined wings and golden eyes. Its larvae are fierce "aphid lions".
entries.f: Lacewings lay each egg on top of a thin silk stalk to keep it away from hungry predators.

entries.t: A master of disguise that looks — and even sways — like a twig in the breeze.
entries.f: Some stick insect species can reproduce without any males.

entries.t: An aerial hunter that can fly in every direction and catches most of the prey it chases.
entries.f: Dragonfly relatives 300 million years ago had wingspans of about 70 cm.

entries.t: A slender cousin of the dragonfly that folds its wings along its back when resting.
entries.f: Damselfly young live underwater for months, breathing through gills at the tips of their tails.

entries.t: An orange-and-black traveller that migrates up to 4,000 km to spend the winter in Mexican mountain forests.
entries.f: Milkweed toxins stored from its caterpillar days make the monarch poisonous to birds.

entries.t: A velvety black butterfly slashed with scarlet bands, often seen sipping fallen fruit in autumn.
entries.f: Red admirals are strong migrants, flying north across Europe each spring.

entries.t: A dusky brown butterfly decorated with yellow-ringed eyespots. It keeps flying even on cloudy days.
entries.f: Ringlet females scatter their eggs while flying over grass instead of placing them on leaves.

entries.t: A common white butterfly with dark wingtips, whose green caterpillars munch cabbage and broccoli.
entries.f: Originally European, it hitched rides with people to North America, Australia and New Zealand.

entries.t: A sunshine-yellow butterfly that often gathers in groups at puddles to sip minerals.
entries.f: The word "butterfly" may come from butter-yellow species like these.

entries.t: A tiny butterfly with shimmering wings. Many of its caterpillars are guarded by ants in exchange for sweet droplets.
entries.f: Large blue caterpillars trick ants into carrying them into their nest — then eat the ant grubs.

entries.t: The architect of the classic wheel-shaped web. Many orb weavers eat their web each night and spin a fresh one.
entries.f: Weight for weight, spider silk is stronger than steel.

entries.t: A glossy black spider with a red hourglass on its belly. Drop for drop, its venom is stronger than a rattlesnake's.
entries.f: Despite its reputation, bites are rare, and deaths are very rare with modern medical care.

entries.t: A huge, hairy spider that hunts on the ground at night. Some flick barbed hairs from their abdomen at attackers.
entries.f: Female tarantulas of some species live for 30 years or more.

entries.t: A web-less hunter that runs down its prey. Mothers carry their spiderlings piled on their backs.
entries.f: Sweep a torch across a lawn at night and wolf spider eyes glitter back like tiny diamonds.

entries.t: Often mistaken for a spider, this "daddy longlegs" has one fused body, two eyes, and no silk or venom.
entries.f: If grabbed, a harvestman can shed a leg, which keeps twitching to distract the attacker.

entries.t: A tiny eight-legged hitchhiker that waits on grass tips with its front legs outstretched — a behaviour called "questing".
entries.f: A feeding female tick can swell to about 100 times her unfed weight.

entries.t: A fast-running hunter that injects venom through a pair of modified front legs called forcipules.
entries.f: No centipede has exactly 100 legs — they always have an odd number of leg pairs.

entries.t: One of the fastest runners for its size — so quick that it briefly goes blind while chasing prey.
entries.f: Scaled up to human size, a tiger beetle would sprint at hundreds of kilometres per hour.

entries.t: A shiny night patroller that hunts slugs and caterpillars. There are over 40,000 kinds.
entries.f: Bombardier beetles, a type of ground beetle, fire a boiling chemical spray from their rear.

entries.t: Named for its extraordinarily long antennae, sometimes several times the length of its body.
entries.f: Its larvae bore through wood for years before emerging as adults.

entries.t: A small, often metallic beetle that munches leaves. The Colorado potato beetle is its most infamous member.
entries.f: Golden tortoise beetles, a kind of leaf beetle, can change from gold to red in minutes.

entries.t: A tireless recycler that rolls balls of dung many times its own weight to feed its young.
entries.f: Some dung beetles steer at night using the glow of the Milky Way.

entries.t: A horned heavyweight that uses its horn to flip rivals off branches in battles over mates.
entries.f: For their size, rhinoceros beetles are among the strongest animals on the planet.

entries.t: A beetle with a long snout tipped with tiny jaws, used to bore into seeds, nuts and grain.
entries.f: With tens of thousands of species, weevils form one of the largest animal families on Earth.

entries.t: A mostly microscopic worm so abundant that around four of every five animals on Earth may be nematodes.
entries.f: The nematode C. elegans was the first animal to have its whole genome sequenced.

entries.h: Damp logs and gardens; sea floors
entries.t: A crustacean that moved onto land. Pill bugs roll into armoured balls when threatened.
entries.f: The giant isopod of the deep sea grows to about 50 cm and can survive years without food in captivity.

entries.t: A leggy wader that feeds upside-down, filtering tiny shrimp and algae through its beak.
entries.f: Flamingos hatch grey — their pink colour comes from pigments in their food.

entries.t: A big-billed fisher whose stretchy throat pouch can scoop up more water than its stomach can hold.
entries.f: Brown pelicans plunge-dive headfirst from heights of up to 20 metres to catch fish.

entries.h: Farmland and wetlands of Europe & Africa
entries.t: A tall bird famous in folklore for delivering babies. It builds huge nests on rooftops and chimneys.
entries.f: Nearly voiceless, white storks "talk" by loudly clattering their bills.

entries.t: A shy, glossy-black stork with a red bill that hides in deep forests, unlike its rooftop-loving cousin.
entries.f: Its black feathers shimmer purple and green in the sunlight.

entries.t: A wader with a flat, spoon-shaped bill that it sweeps side to side through water to snap up prey by touch.
entries.f: The roseate spoonbill gets its pink colour the same way flamingos do — from its food.

entries.t: A slate-blue heron that stalks slowly through the shallows. Strangely, its young are pure white for their first year.
entries.f: White youngsters often mix into flocks of snowy egrets, which may help protect them.

entries.t: An elegant all-white heron that stands still as a statue before spearing fish with its dagger bill.
entries.f: Its lacy plumes were so prized for hats that it was nearly wiped out, sparking early bird-protection laws.

entries.t: A camouflaged heron that points its bill skyward and sways with the reeds to vanish from sight.
entries.f: The male Eurasian bittern's booming call can carry up to 5 km.

entries.t: A towering bird whose pairs perform elaborate leaping, bowing dances. Many species mate for life.
entries.f: In Japan, folding 1,000 paper cranes is said to grant a wish.

entries.t: A wading bird that feeds almost entirely on apple snails, using a slightly twisted bill to pry out the meat.
entries.f: Its haunting, wailing scream earned it the nickname "crying bird".

entries.t: A busy shorebird that races the waves, probing the sand with its bill for worms and tiny crabs.
entries.f: The bar-tailed godwit, a sandpiper relative, flies over 11,000 km nonstop on migration.

entries.t: A noisy black-and-white shorebird with a carrot-orange bill for hammering or stabbing open shellfish.
entries.f: Young oystercatchers learn their parents' shell-opening technique — hammering or stabbing.

entries.h: Slow rivers and ponds of Europe
entries.t: An olive-green, red-eyed fish of weedy ponds. Its tiny scales are wrapped in thick slime.
entries.f: Folklore called it the "doctor fish", claiming its slime could heal other fish.

entries.t: A silver ocean fish that returns to the very stream where it hatched to spawn, turning red as it goes.
entries.f: Salmon find their home river by remembering the smell of its water.

entries.t: An armoured "living fossil" whose lineage dates back to the dinosaurs. It vacuums food from riverbeds with toothless lips.
entries.f: The beluga sturgeon can live over 100 years and weigh more than a tonne.

entries.h: Rivers and swamps of North America
entries.t: A long, needle-toothed ambusher armoured in diamond-shaped scales once used by Native Americans as arrowheads.
entries.f: Gars can gulp air, letting them survive in warm, oxygen-poor water.

entries.t: A freshwater cousin of the lobster that shoots backwards with a flick of its tail when startled.
entries.f: Crayfish can regrow lost claws and legs when they moult.

entries.h: Rivers and ponds of North America & Eurasia
entries.t: Nature's engineer, felling trees with iron-strengthened orange teeth to build dams and lodges.
entries.f: Beaver ponds create wetlands that support hundreds of other species.

entries.t: A sleek, playful swimmer that closes its ears and nostrils underwater. Sea otters hold paws while sleeping so they don't drift apart.
entries.f: Sea otters have the densest fur of any animal — up to about 150,000 hairs per square centimetre.

entries.t: A sleek, semi-aquatic hunter with oily, waterproof fur, equally at home chasing fish or rabbits.
entries.f: American mink that escaped from fur farms now live wild across much of Europe.

entries.t: A diving duck with a shaggy crest and a thin, saw-toothed bill for gripping slippery fish.
entries.f: Its serrated bill gives mergansers the nickname "sawbills".

entries.h: Ponds and marshes of the Americas
entries.t: A dark, chicken-like water bird with a white bill. Its lobed toes work as paddles in water and snowshoes on mud.
entries.f: Coots aren't ducks at all — they're related to rails and cranes.

entries.h: Reedy marshes of Europe, Africa & Asia
entries.t: A glossy purple-blue marsh bird with a red forehead shield and oversized feet for walking on floating plants.
entries.f: It holds food up to its bill with one foot, almost like a parrot.

entries.t: A giant frog with a deep, cow-like "jug-o-rum" call. It eats almost anything it can fit in its mouth — even snakes.
entries.f: In male bullfrogs, the eardrum is bigger than the eye.

entries.t: A climbing frog with sticky toe pads that let it cling to leaves — and even glass.
entries.f: Some tree frogs can shift colour from green to brown to match their surroundings.

entries.h: Cold mountain streams of NW North America
entries.t: A small frog of icy, rushing streams. It has no eardrums and no croak — useless over the roar of water.
entries.f: The "tail" is found only on males and is used in mating, a feature unique among frogs.

entries.t: A black-and-yellow salamander whose bright colours warn of toxic skin secretions.
entries.f: Its name comes from legends of salamanders crawling out of burning logs — they had been hiding inside.

entries.t: A small salamander that returns to ponds to breed. Young of some species live on land as bright orange "efts".
entries.f: Newts can regrow lost legs, tails, parts of their eyes and even heart tissue.

entries.t: A black salamander with yellow polka dots that emerges in great numbers on rainy spring nights to breed.
entries.f: Algae live inside its eggs — and even its cells — making it partly solar-powered.

entries.t: A smiling salamander that never grows up, keeping its feathery gills and living underwater its whole life.
entries.f: Critically endangered in the wild, axolotls can regrow limbs, spinal cord and even parts of the brain.

entries.t: A sun-loving turtle that basks on logs to warm up, then plops into the water at the first sign of danger.
entries.f: Some turtles overwinter underwater, absorbing oxygen through their skin and rear end.

entries.t: A land turtle with a hinged lower shell that closes up tight like a box.
entries.f: Box turtles can live for more than 100 years.

entries.t: A wall-walking lizard whose toes carry millions of microscopic hairs that grip almost any surface.
entries.f: Most geckos can't blink — they lick their eyes to keep them clean.

entries.t: A big green lizard with a spiny crest that basks in treetops and drops into rivers to escape danger.
entries.f: Iguanas have a light-sensing "third eye" on top of their heads.

entries.h: Trees and gardens of the SE USA & Caribbean
entries.t: A small lizard that flashes a pink throat fan called a dewlap to claim territory. It can shift from green to brown.
entries.f: Anoles are nicknamed "American chameleons", but they aren't chameleons at all.

entries.h: Deserts and grasslands of the Americas
entries.t: A fast, restless lizard with a long whip-like tail, constantly on the move hunting insects.
entries.f: Some whiptail species are all-female and reproduce by cloning.

entries.t: A sun-loving rock lizard. The male rainbow agama flaunts a fiery orange head and electric-blue body.
entries.f: Male agamas bob their heads like push-ups to impress females and warn rivals.

entries.t: A stiff-scaled lizard with a long body and short legs, named for its alligator-like armour.
entries.f: A soft fold of skin along each side lets its armoured body expand when it eats or breathes.

entries.t: A brilliant emerald lizard of European meadows. In spring, the males' throats turn vivid blue.
entries.f: Like many lizards, it can drop its tail to escape a predator and grow it back.

entries.t: A slow-motion lizard with swivelling eyes that look two ways at once, and a tongue that shoots out faster than a blink.
entries.f: Chameleons change colour mainly to communicate and control temperature, not just to hide.

entries.t: The largest living lizard, a powerful ambush hunter with a venomous bite.
entries.f: Female Komodo dragons can lay fertile eggs without a male.

entries.t: An armoured river giant that lurks with only its eyes and nostrils above the water.
entries.f: Crocodile mothers gently carry their hatchlings to the water in their huge jaws.

entries.h: Swamps of the SE United States
entries.t: A broad-snouted swamp king that bellows so deeply the water dances on its back.
entries.f: The temperature of the nest decides whether hatchlings are male or female.

entries.h: Moist forests of the eastern USA
entries.t: A tiny, glossy snake that burrows like an earthworm and pokes with its pointed tail if picked up.
entries.f: Harmless to people, it spends most of its life hidden under logs and in soil.

entries.t: A slender snake with a golden collar that curls its tail to flash a red-orange belly when threatened.
entries.f: It is mildly venomous to its small prey but harmless to people.

entries.t: A dramatic actor that flattens its neck and hisses like a cobra — and if that fails, rolls over and plays dead.
entries.f: Its upturned snout works like a shovel for digging up toads.

entries.t: A slender, leaf-green snake that vanishes into grass and vines while hunting crickets and caterpillars.
entries.f: It is one of the few snakes that eats mostly insects.

entries.t: A powerful constrictor named "king" because it eats other snakes — including venomous rattlesnakes.
entries.f: Kingsnakes are largely resistant to rattlesnake venom.

entries.t: One of the most common snakes in North America, striped like old-fashioned sock garters.
entries.f: Each spring tens of thousands emerge together from the Narcisse snake dens in Manitoba, Canada.

entries.t: A thick-bodied swimmer often mistaken for the venomous cottonmouth, though it is harmless.
entries.f: Water snakes give birth to live young — sometimes dozens at once.

entries.t: A whip-thin snake that looks exactly like a hanging vine as it waits for lizards to pass.
entries.f: Asian vine snakes have grooves on their snouts that let them see forward in 3D to strike accurately.

entries.h: Deserts and scrub of western North America
entries.t: A small, spotted snake with cat-like vertical pupils that hunts sleeping lizards after dark.
entries.f: Its mild venom, delivered by rear fangs, is harmless to humans.

entries.t: A heavy-bodied constrictor that tightens its coils each time its prey breathes out, stopping blood flow.
entries.f: Boas give birth to live young, sometimes more than 60 at a time.

entries.t: Africa's largest snake, strong enough to swallow an antelope whole.
entries.f: Mother pythons coil around their eggs to guard them until they hatch.

entries.h: Fields and forests of South Asia
entries.t: A hooded snake that rears up and spreads its neck ribs when threatened, showing the famous "spectacle" mark.
entries.f: It is one of India's "Big Four" snakes responsible for most snakebites there.

entries.t: A shy, emerald tree snake that glides among the branches. Its bite is dangerously venomous.
entries.f: Unlike its cousin the black mamba, it usually flees rather than confronting people.

entries.h: Pinewoods of the SE United States
entries.t: The heaviest venomous snake in the Americas, warning intruders with the dry buzz of its rattle.
entries.f: A new rattle segment is added each time it sheds its skin.

entries.t: The ocean's most famous predator. Jelly-filled pores on its snout sense the faint electric fields of hidden prey.
entries.f: Great whites sometimes leap completely out of the water to ambush seals.

entries.t: A striped "garbage can of the sea" — turtles, birds and even licence plates have been found in its stomach.
entries.f: Its stripes fade as it grows older.

entries.t: A shark with a wide, hammer-shaped head that sweeps the sand like a metal detector for buried stingrays.
entries.f: Its wide-set eyes give it an excellent all-round view.

entries.t: A soft, round ray that stuns prey with electric shocks of up to 220 volts.
entries.f: Ancient Greeks and Romans used electric rays to numb pain.

entries.t: A flat fish that buries itself in sand with only its eyes poking out. The venomous barb on its tail is for defence only.
entries.f: Shuffle your feet when wading — stingrays feel the vibration and glide away.

entries.t: A big-headed sea turtle whose powerful jaws crush crabs and conchs. It crosses entire oceans in its lifetime.
entries.f: Hatchlings use Earth's magnetic field like a built-in map.

entries.t: The largest turtle on Earth, with a rubbery, ridged shell instead of hard plates. It dives deeper than 1,000 metres.
entries.f: Its throat is lined with backward-pointing spines that stop slippery jellyfish escaping.

entries.t: A snake fully adapted to life at sea, with a paddle-shaped tail for swimming. Many are highly venomous.
entries.f: Some sea snakes absorb oxygen through their skin, allowing very long dives.

entries.t: The largest dolphin, a black-and-white hunter living in close family pods that each have their own "dialect".
entries.f: Orcas are apex predators that even hunt great white sharks.

entries.t: A barnacle-crusted giant that rolls on its side to suck up mud and filter out tiny crustaceans.
entries.f: It makes one of the longest migrations of any mammal — up to 20,000 km round trip.

entries.t: A gentle "sea cow" that grazes on seagrass meadows. Sailors' sightings may have inspired mermaid legends.
entries.f: Dugongs are more closely related to elephants than to whales or seals.

entries.t: A barking, playful swimmer that "walks" on land by turning its rear flippers forward — something true seals can't do.
entries.f: Sea lions have visible ear flaps; true seals just have ear holes.

entries.t: A master glider with the largest wingspan of any living bird, able to soar for hours without flapping.
entries.f: Wisdom, a Laysan albatross, was still laying eggs past the age of 70.

entries.t: A long, silvery predator with fang-like teeth, known as snoek in South Africa.
entries.f: It is often confused with the barracuda, but the two aren't closely related.

entries.t: A snake-shaped fish that can wriggle short distances over wet land. European eels cross the Atlantic to breed.
entries.f: No one has ever watched European eels spawn in the wild — it remains a mystery.

entries.t: A drifting bell with no brain, heart or bones — it's about 95% water.
entries.f: Turritopsis dohrnii can revert to its youthful stage, earning it the name "immortal jellyfish".

entries.t: A flower-like animal that waves stinging tentacles to catch passing prey, then pulls it into its central mouth.
entries.f: Clownfish shelter among its tentacles, protected by a special mucus coat.

entries.t: A reef-builder whose grooved dome looks just like a human brain. It is made of thousands of tiny animals called polyps.
entries.f: Some brain corals live for hundreds of years.

entries.t: A ribbon-thin worm that glides on a carpet of tiny hairs. Marine species ripple in dazzling warning colours.
entries.f: Cut a planarian flatworm into pieces and each piece can regrow into a whole worm.

entries.t: A sea snail with a flaring, pink-lipped shell. Hold one to your ear, and people say you hear the ocean.
entries.f: Queen conchs can make natural pearls, which are pink and very rare.

entries.t: A shell-less snail painted in neon colours. Some steal stinging cells from their prey to use as their own defence.
entries.f: "Nudibranch" means "naked gills" — the feathery tufts on its back.

entries.t: An oval mollusc armoured with eight overlapping plates. Pried off a rock, it curls up like a pill bug.
entries.f: Some chitons have hundreds of tiny eyes with mineral lenses built into their shell plates.

entries.t: A "living fossil" in a striped spiral shell that adjusts the gas in its chambers to rise and sink like a submarine.
entries.f: A nautilus has up to 90 tentacles but no suckers.

entries.t: A sideways-scuttling crustacean in a hard shell, with claws for cracking, digging and fighting.
entries.f: Crabs must moult their whole shell to grow, hiding while the new one hardens.

entries.t: The male waves one enormous claw like a fiddler's bow to attract mates and warn rivals.
entries.f: In some species, if a male loses his big claw, the small one grows huge instead.

entries.t: A soft-bodied crab that moves into empty snail shells, trading up for bigger homes as it grows.
entries.f: Hermit crabs sometimes line up by size to swap shells in a "vacancy chain".

entries.t: Clawed lobsters carry a crusher claw and a cutter claw; spiny lobsters defend themselves with long, spiky antennae.
entries.f: Lobsters taste with their legs and have blue blood.

entries.t: A five-armed hunter that pries open clams and pushes its stomach out of its mouth to digest them.
entries.f: Starfish have a simple eye at the tip of each arm.

entries.t: A living pincushion that walks on hundreds of tube feet and chews algae with a five-toothed jaw called "Aristotle's lantern".
entries.f: Some sea urchins live for more than 100 years.

entries.t: A squishy vacuum cleaner of the sea floor. When threatened, some shoot out sticky threads — or even their own guts.
entries.f: Pearlfish sometimes live inside sea cucumbers — entering through their bottoms.

entries.t: A bright orange fish that lives safely among the stinging tentacles of sea anemones.
entries.f: Clownfish are born male; the dominant fish in a group can become female.

entries.h: Indo-Pacific reefs; invasive in the Atlantic
entries.t: A striped fish fanning out venomous spines like a lion's mane. It corners prey with its wide fins.
entries.f: Released aquarium lionfish have invaded the Caribbean, where divers hunt them to protect reefs.

entries.t: A slow swimmer that gulps water to balloon into a spiky ball too big to swallow.
entries.f: Many puffers contain a toxin far deadlier than cyanide — yet specially licensed chefs in Japan serve it as "fugu".

entries.t: A striking yellow-and-black angelfish of Caribbean reefs that feeds mainly on sponges.
entries.f: Juveniles are yellow with a single black spot that grows into a large black patch.

entries.h: Lakes and coasts of North America
entries.t: A mighty fish-snatching eagle and the national bird of the USA, recovered from near extinction.
entries.f: Bald eagles build the largest nests of any North American bird — one weighed about 2 tonnes.

entries.h: Towns, rivers and fields of the Old World
entries.t: A fork-tailed raptor that soars over cities and markets, snatching scraps with remarkable agility.
entries.f: In Australia, "firehawk" kites have been seen spreading bushfires by carrying burning sticks.

entries.t: Nature's clean-up crew. Powerful stomach acid lets it safely eat carcasses that would sicken other animals.
entries.f: A Rüppell's vulture holds the record for the highest-flying bird, at about 11,300 m.

entries.t: A huge, ghostly owl with a dish-shaped face that funnels sound, letting it hear voles tunnelling beneath deep snow.
entries.f: It is one of the tallest owls, but much of its bulk is fluffy feathers.

entries.h: Forests and farmland of South Asia; parks
entries.t: The male fans a shimmering train of around 200 eye-spotted feathers to dazzle females.
entries.f: The Indian peafowl is the national bird of India.

entries.t: A plump ground bird whose males gather at dawn "leks" to strut, puff up and display for females.
entries.f: The ruffed grouse drums its wings so fast it makes a low thump like a distant engine.

entries.t: The only songbird that swims — it walks underwater along stream beds, gripping stones to hunt insect larvae.
entries.f: A see-through third eyelid lets it see clearly underwater.

entries.h: Open country of Africa, Asia & Europe
entries.t: A rainbow-feathered aerial hunter that catches bees mid-flight, then whacks them on a branch to remove the sting.
entries.f: Bee-eaters nest in tunnels they dig into sandy riverbanks.

entries.t: A large, skulking cuckoo with chestnut wings and a deep, booming "hoop-hoop" call.
entries.f: Unlike many cuckoos, coucals raise their own chicks — in some species the male does most of the work.

entries.h: Savannas of Africa; Gir Forest, India
entries.t: The only truly social big cat, living in family groups called prides. Its roar carries up to 8 km.
entries.f: Lionesses do most of the hunting, often working as a team.

entries.t: The fastest land animal, reaching about 100 km/h in a few seconds. Black "tear lines" help cut the sun's glare.
entries.f: Cheetahs can't roar — instead they chirp, purr and yelp.

entries.t: A secretive, rosetted cat strong enough to haul prey heavier than itself up into a tree.
entries.f: Most "black panthers" are leopards with dark fur — the spots are still there.

entries.t: A striped wild horse. No two zebras share the same stripe pattern.
entries.f: Studies suggest the stripes help deter biting flies.

entries.t: The largest land animal. Its trunk has tens of thousands of muscles and can lift logs or pluck a single blade of grass.
entries.f: Elephants flap their huge ears to cool their blood.

entries.t: A massive river-dweller that spends the day submerged and comes ashore to graze at night.
entries.f: Hippos ooze a reddish "blood sweat" that acts as a natural sunscreen.

entries.t: A bone-crushing hunter with one of the strongest bites of any mammal. Spotted hyenas "giggle" when stressed.
entries.f: Spotted hyenas live in female-led clans, and the females are larger than the males.

entries.t: A "painted wolf" with a unique patchwork coat. Packs hunt with one of the highest success rates of any predator.
entries.f: Pack members "vote" on when to set off hunting — by sneezing.

entries.t: A tusked wild pig that kneels on padded knees to graze and reverses into burrows so its tusks face out.
entries.f: The "warts" are thick pads of skin that protect its face during fights.

entries.t: A graceful antelope that "pronks" — springing high on stiff legs — to show predators it's too fit to chase.
entries.f: Some gazelles can go their whole lives without drinking, getting water from plants.

entries.t: An agile antelope that can leap 3 metres high and 10 metres long, scattering its herd to confuse predators.
entries.f: Impalas groom each other in turns — you scratch mine, I'll scratch yours.

entries.t: A long-faced antelope with bracket-shaped horns and a high-shouldered, sloping back.
entries.f: Hartebeest post sentries on termite mounds to watch for predators.

entries.t: A tiny sentinel that stands tall on its hind legs to watch for eagles while its gang forages.
entries.f: Meerkats have different alarm calls for threats from the air and from the ground.

entries.t: A quick, fearless hunter famous for facing down cobras with lightning dodges.
entries.f: Special nerve receptors make mongooses partly resistant to snake venom.

entries.t: The largest bird on Earth. It can't fly, but can sprint at about 70 km/h.
entries.f: An ostrich's eye is bigger than its brain.

entries.t: A stately ground bird of open plains. The great bustard is among the heaviest flying birds in the world.
entries.f: Displaying male great bustards turn their feathers inside-out into a white "foam bath".

entries.h: Forests and mountains of the north
entries.t: A humped powerhouse that fattens up on salmon and berries before sleeping through the winter.
entries.f: The Kodiak bear, a brown bear subspecies, is one of the largest land carnivores.

entries.t: A skilled tree-climber that isn't always black — its coat can be brown, cinnamon or even creamy white.
entries.f: The white "spirit bears" of Canada's rainforest are black bears with a rare gene.

entries.t: A cooperative hunter living in family packs. Howls help members find each other across great distances.
entries.f: Every domestic dog descends from ancient wolves.

entries.t: One of the world's most endangered canids, with only a few dozen roaming wild in North Carolina.
entries.f: The look-alike maned wolf of South America is neither wolf nor fox, but a unique canid of its own.

entries.h: Deserts to cities of North America
entries.t: A clever, adaptable canid that has spread across North America and now lives in cities like Chicago and Los Angeles.
entries.f: Coyotes sometimes team up with badgers to hunt ground squirrels.

entries.t: A cunning hunter with a white-tipped tail. It pounces on mice hidden under snow by listening for them.
entries.f: Foxes may use Earth's magnetic field to aim — their most successful pounces face north-east.

entries.t: A salt-and-pepper fox with curved claws that lets it climb trees like a cat.
entries.f: It is one of the only canids able to climb trees.

entries.t: A tuft-eared forest cat with huge furry paws that work like snowshoes.
entries.f: Canada lynx numbers rise and fall in a roughly 10-year cycle with snowshoe hares.

entries.h: Mountains and forests of the Americas
entries.t: A powerful, solitary cat that can leap about 5 metres straight up into a tree.
entries.f: Puma, mountain lion, panther, catamount — it holds the record for the animal with the most names.

entries.h: Forests of Europe, Asia & North Africa
entries.t: The bristly wild ancestor of the farm pig. Its striped piglets blend into the forest floor.
entries.f: Wild boar mothers raise their piglets together in groups called sounders.

entries.t: A stripe-faced digger that builds huge underground homes called setts, used by generation after generation.
entries.f: Some badger setts are thought to be centuries old.

entries.t: A slim, fierce hunter small enough to chase mice down their own tunnels.
entries.f: The least weasel is the smallest carnivore on Earth.

entries.t: A chunky ground squirrel of alpine meadows that whistles shrill alarms when eagles circle overhead.
entries.f: Marmots can hibernate for up to eight months a year.

entries.t: A mountain sheep whose rams clash curling horns at around 30 km/h in head-butting contests.
entries.f: A ram's horns can weigh more than all the bones in its body.

entries.t: A wild goat with enormous ridged horns that climbs near-vertical cliffs — even dam walls — to lick salt.
entries.f: Once hunted down to about 100 animals, ibex now number in the tens of thousands.

entries.h: Prairies of North America; European forests
entries.t: The heaviest land animal of North America, a shaggy giant that can still sprint at about 55 km/h.
entries.f: Bison roll in dusty "wallows" to shed fur and fend off insects.

entries.t: The "ghost of the mountains", a smoky-grey cat that wraps its thick tail around itself like a scarf.
entries.f: Snow leopards can't roar; they greet each other with a puffing "chuff".

entries.t: A fiery-furred tree climber with a ringed tail. It was called "panda" before the giant panda was.
entries.f: Like the giant panda, it has a "false thumb" — an extended wrist bone for gripping bamboo.

entries.t: A black-and-white bear that spends up to 14 hours a day munching bamboo.
entries.f: A newborn panda is about 1/900th of its mother's weight — roughly the size of a stick of butter.

entries.t: The largest tree-dwelling animal, a thoughtful red ape whose name means "person of the forest" in Malay.
entries.f: Orangutans build a fresh leafy nest high in the trees to sleep in every night.

entries.t: The largest primate. A silverback leads its family group and beats its chest to show strength.
entries.f: Gorillas share about 98% of their DNA with humans.

entries.t: A clever ape that makes tools — stripping twigs to fish termites from mounds and cracking nuts with stones.
entries.f: Chimpanzees and bonobos are our closest living relatives.

entries.t: An acrobatic "lesser ape" that swings arm-over-arm through the canopy at up to 55 km/h.
entries.f: Gibbon pairs sing loud duets each morning to defend their territory.

entries.t: The largest gibbon, with an inflatable throat sac that booms its song across the forest.
entries.f: Siamang songs can be heard 2–3 km away.

entries.h: Asia & North Africa, forests to cities
entries.t: A bold, adaptable monkey that thrives everywhere from snowy mountains to busy temples.
entries.f: Japanese macaques warm up in hot springs during snowy winters.

entries.h: Forests and towns of South & SE Asia
entries.t: A long-tailed, leaf-eating monkey with a black face, often seen lounging around temples.
entries.f: Langurs have multi-chambered stomachs, a bit like cows, to digest tough leaves.

entries.t: A black-and-white monkey with a flowing white cape that streams behind it as it leaps between trees.
entries.f: "Colobus" means "mutilated" in Greek, because it has only a stub for a thumb.

entries.t: A pot-bellied monkey whose males sport an enormous drooping nose to amplify their calls.
entries.f: It is an excellent swimmer, with partly webbed feet.

entries.t: A squirrel-sized monkey with ear tufts that gnaws holes in trees to feed on sap and gum.
entries.f: Marmosets usually have twins, and the fathers help carry them.

entries.t: A clever monkey that uses stones as hammers and anvils to crack open nuts.
entries.f: It is named after Capuchin friars, whose hooded robes resembled its cap of fur.

entries.t: One of the loudest land animals — its roars can carry up to 5 km through the rainforest.
entries.f: Howlers use their tails as a fifth hand to grip branches.

entries.t: A fluffy, soft-voiced monkey whose bonded pairs sit side by side with their tails entwined.
entries.f: Titi partners become stressed when separated from each other.

entries.t: A lanky acrobat with a gripping tail so strong it can hang by it alone.
entries.f: The underside of its tail has a hairless, fingerprint-like pad for better grip.

entries.t: A small, bright-eyed monkey that travels in noisy troops that can number in the hundreds.
entries.f: For its body size, it has one of the largest brains of any primate.

entries.h: Savannas and hills of Africa & Arabia
entries.t: A dog-faced monkey living in large troops full of complex friendships and rivalries.
entries.f: Baboons have learned to tell real English words from made-up ones.

entries.t: The fastest primate, a long-legged monkey that can dash across grassland at about 55 km/h.
entries.f: Patas monkeys spend most of their time on the ground rather than in trees.

entries.t: A colourful, long-tailed monkey whose bold face markings may help each species recognise its own kind.
entries.f: Some monkeys in this family have different alarm calls for leopards, eagles and snakes.

entries.t: A sunbathing primate that raises its black-and-white striped tail like a flag to keep its troop together.
entries.f: Males have "stink fights", wafting scented tails at each other.

entries.t: The largest living lemur, whose eerie, whale-like song echoes across Madagascar's forests.
entries.f: Indris don't survive in captivity — the only way to see one is in the wild.

entries.t: The largest cat on Earth. Each tiger's stripes are unique — and even its skin is striped.
entries.f: Unlike most cats, tigers love water and are strong swimmers.

entries.t: The Americas' biggest cat, with a bite strong enough to pierce turtle shells.
entries.f: Jaguar rosettes often have small spots inside them — a leopard's usually don't.

entries.t: The slowest mammal, hanging upside down so still that algae grows in its fur and tints it green.
entries.f: Sloths climb down only about once a week — to go to the toilet.

entries.h: Forests and grasslands of South & SE Asia
entries.t: A small-eared elephant revered across Asia, with a single "finger" at the tip of its trunk.
entries.f: Only some male Asian elephants grow tusks.

entries.t: A shaggy bear that vacuums termites out of their mounds through a gap in its front teeth.
entries.f: Mothers carry their cubs on their backs for months.

entries.t: A rust-red "whistling dog" that hunts in packs and calls to its clan with bird-like whistles.
entries.f: Dholes are endangered, with only a few thousand left in the wild.

entries.t: An armoured digger. The three-banded armadillo can roll itself into a near-perfect ball.
entries.f: Nine-banded armadillos almost always give birth to identical quadruplets.

entries.t: A rainforest bird with a gigantic, colourful bill that is surprisingly light — mostly hollow.
entries.f: Toucans use their big bills like radiators to shed body heat.

entries.t: A dazzling, long-tailed parrot that cracks hard nuts with its powerful beak and flies in noisy pairs.
entries.f: Macaws eat clay from riverbanks, possibly for sodium or to neutralise toxins.

entries.t: A big-billed bird topped with a helmet-like casque. The female seals herself inside a tree hole to nest.
entries.f: The great hornbill is the state bird of Kerala, India.

entries.h: Tropical forests of Central & South America
entries.t: A glittering, long-billed bird that snaps butterflies and dragonflies right out of the air.
entries.f: Jacamars beat captured butterflies against a branch to knock off the wings.

entries.t: A sleepy marsupial that dozes up to 20 hours a day to save energy from its low-nutrient diet.
entries.f: Koala fingerprints are almost identical to human ones.

entries.t: A smaller cousin of the kangaroo that bounds on powerful hind legs and balances with its thick tail.
entries.f: Joeys are born about the size of a jellybean and crawl into their mother's pouch.

entries.t: A stocky burrowing marsupial whose backwards-facing pouch keeps dirt out while it digs.
entries.f: Wombats produce cube-shaped poop.

entries.t: An egg-laying mammal with a duck bill, beaver tail and otter feet. It hunts with eyes closed, sensing the electric signals of prey.
entries.f: Males have venomous spurs, and platypus fur glows under UV light.

entries.t: A spiny, egg-laying mammal that slurps ants with a long, sticky tongue.
entries.f: A baby echidna is called a "puggle".

entries.t: Australia's wild dog, which rarely barks but howls — and can rotate its wrists to climb.
entries.f: Australia's Dingo Fence stretches over 5,000 km, one of the longest structures on Earth.

entries.t: A jet-black swan with a red bill and white wing tips, the emblem of Western Australia.
entries.f: Europeans long believed all swans were white, so "black swan" came to mean the impossible.

entries.t: A crested parrot that raises its yellow crest when excited. Wild flocks are famously loud and mischievous.
entries.f: Sydney's cockatoos learned to open wheelie bins, and the trick spread between neighbourhoods.

entries.h: Forests and gardens of Australia & the Pacific
entries.t: A rainbow-coloured parrot with a brush-tipped tongue for lapping up nectar and pollen.
entries.f: Lorikeets help pollinate eucalyptus trees as they feed.

entries.h: Woodland of northern Australia & New Guinea
entries.t: When threatened, it flares a huge frill around its neck, gapes its mouth — then sprints off on its hind legs.
entries.f: The frill is a flap of skin held up by long spines of cartilage.

entries.t: The largest land carnivore, hunting seals from the sea ice. Its fur looks white, but its skin is black.
entries.f: Polar bear hairs are actually hollow and transparent, not white.

entries.t: A fluffy fox whose coat turns snow-white in winter and brown-grey in summer.
entries.f: Its fur is so warm it doesn't start shivering until about −70 °C.

entries.t: A snow-white wolf of the far north that survives months of darkness and bitter cold.
entries.f: Having met so few humans, Arctic wolves are often unafraid of people.

entries.t: The second-largest penguin, with a golden neck patch. It balances its egg on its feet under a warm belly fold.
entries.f: King penguins can dive deeper than 300 metres.

entries.t: A grouse that turns white in winter and grows feathered "snowshoe" feet.
entries.f: Ptarmigan burrow into snowdrifts to sleep, using the snow as insulation.

entries.t: A one-humped "ship of the desert". Its hump stores fat, not water, as an energy reserve.
entries.f: A thirsty camel can drink over 100 litres of water in about 10 minutes.

entries.t: A tiny desert fox with huge ears that shed heat and pinpoint prey in the dark.
entries.f: It spends hot days underground in dens with several entrances.

entries.h: Deserts of the SW USA & Mexico
entries.t: A bead-scaled, pink-and-black venomous lizard that can survive on just a few big meals a year.
entries.f: A compound in its saliva inspired a medicine for type 2 diabetes.

entries.h: Sandy deserts of the SW USA & Mexico
entries.t: A small rattlesnake that throws its body sideways in S-shaped loops to glide across hot, loose sand.
entries.f: It leaves J-shaped tracks and has horn-like scales over its eyes.

entries.t: A sand-coloured viper with spiky "horns" above its eyes that buries itself in sand to ambush prey.
entries.f: It warns intruders by rubbing its rough scales together to make a rasping sound.

entries.t: An eight-legged hunter armed with grasping pincers and a venomous stinger arched over its back.
entries.f: Scorpions glow bright blue-green under ultraviolet light.

entries.t: A three-horned, frilled giant from the last days of the dinosaurs. Scan a museum skeleton or model to register it.
entries.f: Its skull was among the largest of any land animal — up to about 2.5 m long.

entries.h: Fossil beds — extinct for 252 million years
entries.t: An armoured sea creature that thrived for nearly 300 million years. Scan a fossil to register it.
entries.f: Trilobites had some of the earliest complex eyes, with lenses made of the mineral calcite.
